steps.title: SSH: two proofs, no certificate authority
text: SSH solves the same trust problem as TLS in a different way. This lab uses no certificate authority. SSH can use one, but it does not need one. The client remembers each server's key, and the server checks each user's key.
So SSH asks for two proofs. The server proves itself with its host key. The client proves itself with its own key pair, and this is how a client authenticates to a server in SSH.
SSH is also one of the two ways an old device may reach a new server. Lesson 9 builds on this one.
Built to show the parts. Do not copy.

claims.text: SSH can tie host keys to names with a local database or with a certification authority; this lab pins the host key and uses no CA.
claims.source: RFC 4251, section 4.1 (Host Keys); docs/lesson-ssh-names.md, Events, ssh.hostkey.seen and ssh.hostkey.first-use rows

steps.title: First, hello
text: Each side sends one line of text that says it speaks SSH and names its software. This is the version line.
It travels in the clear. After this line, everything moves in packets.

claims.text: Each SSH side sends an identification string before the binary packet protocol starts.
claims.source: RFC 4253, section 4.2 (Protocol Version Exchange)

steps.title: Pick the tools together
text: Each side sends a KexInit packet. It lists the algorithms it can use for key exchange, host key signatures, locking, and sealing.
The two sides pick the first match. If the lists share nothing, the check named algorithm match fails and the talk ends.

This round uses the set the lab calls Modern: curve25519-sha256, ssh-ed25519, aes128-ctr, and hmac-sha2-256. Modern only means newer than the legacy set. It has no encrypt-then-MAC mode, and it is not the best SSH can do.

claims.text: Each side sends a list of supported algorithms in KEXINIT, and the algorithms are chosen from those lists by a fixed rule.
claims.source: RFC 4253, section 7.1 (Algorithm Negotiation)

claims.text: The name Modern means newer than the legacy suite. The suite has no encrypt-then-MAC mode, and it is no claim of the best SSH can do.
claims.source: docs/lesson-ssh-names.md, What the tour must state, item 6 (branch fix/ssh-verdict, PR #51)

steps.title: Strict key exchange
text: The two sides now say whether they run strict key exchange. In this lab both rounds show it on.

Strict KEX answers an attack called Terrapin (CVE-2023-48795). An attacker removes a packet from the start of the protected stream, and the two sides can end up with some security features turned down without noticing.

A peer that does not offer strict KEX leaves it off, and the event then says off. These two suites still stop the prefix attack in that case, because the seal covers the plain text and a deleted packet moves the cipher stream. An injected Ignore packet can still kill such a session.

claims.text: Terrapin (CVE-2023-48795) lets an attacker bypass integrity checks so that some packets from the start of the handshake are omitted, which can downgrade or disable security features.
claims.source: NVD, CVE-2023-48795, description (read 2026-11-05)

claims.text: Both lab rounds run strict KEX because the glass client and server both offer it. A peer that does not offer it leaves it off. The lab's two suites still stop the prefix attack then (0 of 4,000 accepted on each suite in Jared's sweep), because the MAC covers the plain text. An injected Ignore can still kill such a session.
claims.source: docs/lesson-ssh-names.md, What the tour must state, item 7, and Events, ssh.kex.strict row (branch fix/ssh-verdict, PR #51)

steps.title: The server signs the exchange
text: The key exchange works as in lesson 3: each side sends a public share, and both compute the same secret.

The server's reply adds two things. It sends its host key. It also signs a hash of everything said so far, which includes both shares. The signature shows that whoever holds the host key took part in this very exchange.
Try it: flip one byte of that signature. The client's check named exchange signature fails.

tryIt.label: Flip one byte of the exchange signature

claims.text: The curve25519-sha256 method uses the same message flow and exchange hash structure as the ECDH method in RFC 5656, with Curve25519 as in RFC 7748.
claims.source: RFC 8731, section 3 (Key Exchange Methods)

steps.title: A share that makes a weak secret
text: A bad server can send a share made of all zeros. Then both sides would compute a secret that anyone can compute.
So both sides check that the result of the X25519 step is not all zero. The check is named x25519 result not zero.
Try it: send the all-zero share. The check fails and the talk ends.

claims.text: X25519 gives the all-zero value for an input point of small order, and implementations may check for an all-zero shared secret and abort. SSH curve25519-sha256 uses that check.
claims.source: RFC 7748, section 6.1 (Curve25519); RFC 8731, section 3 (Key Exchange Methods)

steps.title: Whose key is this?
text: The host key card shows the server's key and its fingerprint, a short hash of the key. The client compares the key with the one it saved from an earlier visit. The check is named known_hosts match.

A host key is trusted because the client pinned it earlier. With no pinned key, this client refuses by default. A caller can choose trust on first use, and then must store the key. On that very first connect there is nothing to compare, so the first connect has no proof at all. The fingerprint card is the moment to check the key another way, such as asking the server's owner.
Try it: have the server present a different key. The saved key stays the same, the match fails, and the client stops.

claims.text: SSH has no infrastructure for distributing host keys. A client may accept a host key the first time it connects, save it, and compare it on later connections; connecting without first verifying the key is open to a man-in-the-middle attack.
claims.source: RFC 4251, section 4.1 (Host Keys) and section 9.3.4 (Man-in-the-middle)

claims.text: With no pinned key the client refuses by default (SSH_HOST_KEY_UNKNOWN). Trust on first use is an explicit choice, and the caller must store the key.
claims.source: docs/lesson-ssh-names.md, Events, ssh.hostkey.first-use row (branch fix/ssh-verdict, PR #51)

steps.title: The lock switches on
text: Both sides send NewKeys, and everything after it is sealed. SSH hides the length field inside the sealed packet. TCP segments and timing can still show packet sizes, so a watcher may still guess where packets end.
Try it: switch to the eavesdropper view. Each packet shows only noise and a seal.

claims.text: SSH encrypts the whole packet except the MAC, including the length field. TCP segments and timing can still show packet sizes.
claims.source: RFC 4253, section 6 (Binary Packet Protocol: the packet, excluding the MAC, is encrypted); docs/lesson-ssh-names.md, Fields, Protected packet row, and Richard's note of 2026-11-05 that the tour must not say an eavesdropper sees no packet boundary

steps.title: Every packet carries a seal
text: The receiver checks the seal on each packet. The check is named packet MAC. It passes on the normal run.
Try it: flip one byte of the protected login packet. The seal no longer fits, and the check fails.

tryIt.label: Flip one byte of a protected packet

steps.title: Now the client proves who it is
text: The server has proved itself. Now the client must prove itself. It names a public key, and the server says whether it would accept that key (UserauthQuery, then UserauthPkOk).
Then the client signs a message with the matching private key and sends it (UserauthSigned). The signed data includes the session id, so the signature works for this session only.
The server checks the signature against the public key it allows for this user. The check is named userauth signature verify.
Try it: name the allowed public key but sign with a different private key. The signature does not verify, and the server refuses.

tryIt.label: Sign with the wrong private key

claims.text: In SSH public key authentication, possession of a private key serves as authentication. The client sends a signature made with its private key over data that starts with the session identifier, and the server must check that the key is valid for the user and that the signature is valid.
claims.source: RFC 4252, section 7 (Public Key Authentication Method: publickey)

steps.title: Run one command
text: With the client accepted, it opens a channel and asks the server to run a command. This is the exec request.
The lab's server does not start a process. It answers from a fixed table of two commands, echo and whoami, so the lesson cannot be used to run anything.
A channel holds no more than its window of unread bytes. The window opens again only when the reader reads, so a stalled reader makes the sender wait.

claims.text: An SSH channel request can start a shell, an application program, or a subsystem at the remote end.
claims.source: RFC 4254, section 6.5 (Starting a Shell or a Command)

claims.text: The lab's SSH server has a fixed table of two commands, echo and whoami, and starts no process.
claims.source: docs/lesson-ssh-names.md, What the tour must state, item 5 (branch feat/s4-ssh); docs/program-design.md, section 2.6, SSH-2 paragraph

claims.text: A channel holds no more than its window of unread bytes. The window opens again only when the reader reads, so a stalled reader makes the sender wait.
claims.source: RFC 4254, section 5.2 (Data Transfer: the window size specifies how many bytes the other party can send before it must wait for the window to be adjusted); docs/lesson-ssh-names.md, item 8

steps.title: A tunnel through the server
text: SSH can also carry other traffic. The client asks the server to open a connection to a target and relay it. This is a tunnel.
A server should not relay to just anywhere. The lab keeps an allow list of targets. The server checks the target against it, and the check is named tunnel allow list.
Try it: ask for a tunnel to a target that is off the list. The check fails.

tryIt.label: Ask for a tunnel to a target off the list

claims.text: SSH TCP/IP forwarding uses direct-tcpip channels to open a connection to a host and port, and the receiving side must decide whether to allow the forwarding.
claims.source: RFC 4254, section 7.2 (TCP/IP Forwarding Channels); docs/lesson-ssh-names.md, tunnel allow list row (actor server, branch fix/ssh-followups)

steps.title: The old suite for the old device
text: A second round runs the legacy suite that an older device might use: diffie-hellman-group14-sha1, aes128-cbc, hmac-sha1, and an ssh-rsa host key. Each weak part gets a note at the moment it applies.
SHA-1 has known collision attacks, and the ssh-rsa host key signs with SHA-1. aes128-cbc with a seal over the plain text has a published plaintext recovery attack.
HMAC-SHA-1 is a different case. There is no known practical break of it. It is old, and the modern suite replaces it.
Try it: flip one byte of the RSA signature in this round. The exchange signature check fails, even though round 1 passed.

tryIt.label: Flip one byte of the legacy RSA signature

claims.text: Collision attacks have been used to undermine SHA-1. In 2022 NIST announced that SHA-1 should be phased out by Dec. 31, 2030, and recommended SHA-2 or SHA-3.
claims.source: NIST news, NIST Retires SHA-1 Cryptographic Algorithm, 2022-12-15

claims.text: The ssh-rsa host key format signs with RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 using the SHA-1 hash.
claims.source: RFC 4253, section 6.6 (Public Key Algorithms)

claims.text: Error handling in the SSH protocol in SSH Tectia products and OpenSSH 4.7p1, and possibly other versions, makes it easier for remote attackers to recover certain plaintext data from an arbitrary block of ciphertext when a block cipher in CBC mode is used (CVE-2008-5161).
claims.source: NVD, CVE-2008-5161, description (the published paper by Albrecht, Paterson and Watson, 2009 was not fetched)

claims.text: As of RFC 6194 (2011), there is no indication that attacks on SHA-1 extend to HMAC-SHA-1.
claims.source: RFC 6194, section 3.3 (HMAC-SHA-1)

steps.title: What was tested, and what was not
text: In SSH the server proves itself with a host key the client pinned earlier, and the client proves itself with a signed message. Neither side needs a certificate authority.
The lab shows an old device's SSH suite beside a modern one on the desktop. The code is CF-compiled, run on the desktop CLR, never run on CE. The lab has not touched real CE hardware.
Built to show the parts. Do not copy.

claims.text: In this run, nothing has touched real Windows CE hardware. The engines are compiled for the CF runtime and run on the desktop CLR.
claims.source: docs/prd.md, Spike results table, row 'CE compiler, emulator, device'
